newsitem.title: USA: Boeing begins work of melding corporate cultures.
newsitem.headline: Boeing begins work of melding corporate cultures.

text.p: Boeing Co. brings out the brass bands and balloons Monday to mark the birth of an industry behemoth created by its merger with McDonnell Douglas Corp.

As many of Boeing's 220,000 employees turn out for rallies to kick off the first workweek at what is now the world's largest aerospace company, executives are getting down to the business of merging programmes, reassigning managers and melding two disparate corporate cultures.

The task of integrating more than 60,000 McDonnell Douglas workers is a daunting one, which Boeing executives must complete as they are ramping up commercial jet production to record rates, putting what analysts say is a temporary squeeze on profits.
Boeing already has moved quickly to begin consolidating its commercial operations, installing a longtime sales executive to take over McDonnell Douglas' troubled Douglas Aircraft unit.

Despite seven months of work by transition teams, Boeing Chairman and Chief Executive Officer Phil Condit said Boeing has not yet made any decisions about the future of McDonnell Douglas models such as the MD-95 and MD-11, which have won few orders in recent years amid brutal competition with Boeing and its European rival Airbus Industrie.
Management of Boeing's newly enlarged defence and space business is far less certain.

Condit and President and Chief Operating Officer Harry Stonecipher, formerly of McDonnell Douglas, disagree over where the business should be based and who should run it. Stonecipher favours keeping management of the unit in St. Louis, where McDonnell Douglas was based and its fighter jet factories are located, while Condit would prefer to have the business run from Seattle.
Company officials say a decision might not be announced for several weeks.

Boeing completed the merger early Aug. 1 after scrapping 20-year exclusive contracts to supply jets to three airlines and making other concessions to win approval from the European Commission and avert a trans-Atlantic trade war.

The Federal Trade Commission already had given its blessing, noting that McDonnell Douglas was no longer an effective competitor for commercial jet orders. And the Pentagon enthusiastically backed the merger, hoping for production efficiencies in an age of shrinking weapons budgets.

Condit has said he can save $1 billion in annual costs without substantial layoffs and smooth out the steep hills and valleys of the typical commercial aircraft cycle by adding the many military programmes of McDonnell Douglas, maker of the F-15 Eagle and F/A-18 Hornet fighter jets and C-17 Globemaster air transport.

To do that, Boeing will have to bring its drive to streamline production processes, begun at the end of the last airline industry downturn, to a company more accustomed to the forgiving environment of government contracts.

Larry Bishop, Boeing's vice president for communications and investor relations, said the company plans to do that by building a new corporate culture "rather than just combining existing corporate cultures."

Meanwhile, Boeing executives need to work out hundreds of details large and small, from the future of overlapping programmes and job functions to new paychecks, identification badges and e-mail addresses.

All employees are receiving two-inch-thick "Day One" packets including videos and booklets describing the histories of Boeing and McDonnell Douglas and a common vision as well as lapel pins with the new corporate logo.

After an address in Washington Monday that will be beamed to dozens of the company's plants , Condit and Stonecipher will hit the road, visiting employees in eight states before returning home to Seattle.
